RESEARCH SNAPSHOT6 September 2026Every figure has its own reference period.
ASSESSMENT · 6 SEP 2026

Price pressure. Continued growth. A mixed picture.

Inflation has risen and growth has moderated. Low unemployment coexists with a lower employment rate. The evidence reviewed does not establish that euro adoption caused the broader slowdown or all of the rise in prices.

WHAT CAN BE ATTRIBUTED TO THE EURO?

A small initial price effect

ECB researchers estimated a 0.3–0.4 percentage-point initial inflation effect, concentrated in services. Their preliminary analysis covered January–February 2026; it is not an estimate of the euro’s contribution to August inflation.

They also estimated roughly 0.1 percentage point of additional headline inflation in 2025 from possible advance price adjustments. Retail-chain data did not show systematic upward rounding at the changeover.

Read the ECB research · 9 April 2026 ↗

HOW TO READ THE NUMBERS

After does not establish because

Energy costs, wages, taxes, demand and base effects also influence inflation. The European Commission’s May forecast identified energy costs as an important source of price pressure.

Inflation is a rate of change, not the price level. Lower inflation does not mean prices have fallen. Average gross wages do not describe every household, and comparing quarterly wage growth with a single month’s inflation does not establish real-wage growth.

HICP supports international comparisons; national CPI and the small-basket index measure different baskets. Monthly Eurostat unemployment is seasonally adjusted and differs from quarterly survey figures.
